Unit 2 · 3 / 82
01 · Unit 1 recap · the losses
G, D and their BCE losses
Generator G
noise z → fake image G(z). Wants D to say “real”.
Discriminator D
image → D(·) = chance it is real, 0 … 1 (sigmoid).
L_D = −log D(x) − log(1 − D(G(z)))  ·  L_G = −log D(G(z))
D: real → label 1, fake → label 0  ·  G: its fakes get label 1 (the non-saturating loss)
1
D says 0.9 on a real image: −log 0.9 = 0.105. Small: D is right.
2
D says 0.9 on a fake: −log(1 − 0.9) = −log 0.1 = 2.303. Big: D is fooled.
3
G’s loss on a fake D scored 0.3: −log 0.3 = 1.204. “Getting closer.”
Why we recap this: Unit 2 changes exactly these loss lines.
Unit 2 · 4 / 82
01 · Unit 1 recap · the game
The minimax game and the best D
In plain words: D tries to make the value V big (be right); G tries to make it small (fool D). One game, two players.
min_G max_D V = E[ log D(x) ] + E[ log(1 − D(G(z))) ]
“G minimises, D maximises: the average log-score on real plus the average log of (1 − score) on fakes”
Best D for a frozen G: D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)). Example: 0.6 / (0.6 + 0.2) = 0.75.
Balance: bags match → D* = 0.5 everywhere → V = log 0.5 + log 0.5 = −log 4 = −1.386.
Why it matters: when the bags don’t overlap, this game gives G no useful push.

01 · Unit 1 recap · what broke
What broke at the end of Unit 1
Mode collapse
Every sample is the same digit, e.g. only 7s.
D too strong
D(real) ≈ 0.999, D(fake) ≈ 0.001. Images freeze.
Oscillation
Losses and images swing; nothing settles.
Unit 1 band-aid
What it did
One-sided label smoothing: real label 0.9
stops D getting over-confident
Instance noise, 0.05 × randn, on D’s inputs
blurs real and fake so they overlap
Balanced learning rates (TTUR)
keeps D from running away
Why Unit 2: band-aids treat symptoms; Unit 2 fixes the cause.

1

No overlap. A near-perfect D: ≈ 0 on every fake, ≈ 1 on every real.

Unit 2 · 7 / 82
02 · Why GANs fail · the sweet spot
A narrow sweet spot for D
In plain words: with BCE, D doing its job too well hurts G. D must be “good, but not too good”.
D too weak
D(real) ≈ 0.5, D(fake) ≈ 0.5
L_D ≈ 1.39. Its slope is random: G learns nothing about digits.
Just right
D(real) ≈ 0.6, D(fake) ≈ 0.45
L_D ≈ 1.11. Piles overlap, so D’s slope points to the real pile.
D too strong
D(real) ≈ 0.999, D(fake) ≈ 0.001
L_D ≈ 0.002. Fakes sit on the plateau: no aim.
And D usually drifts to the right. So you spend more time holding D back (label smoothing, TTUR) than training.
Why it matters: keeping D “just right” is hard, so training is fragile.

03 · Measuring distance · wish list
What a good distance must do
Story so far: G’s push dies once D wins. Now: what distance is BCE really measuring?
1
Zero when the two patterns are identical.
2
Never negative. Like a real distance in metres.
3
Bigger when the patterns are more different.
4
Finite. No “infinity” answers.
5
Keeps changing as fakes move closer. This gives G a push.
Why GANs care: rule 5 matters most. No change → no gradient → no learning.

Unit 2 · 14 / 82
03 · Measuring distance · KL 3 / 3
Two problems with KL
1 · Order changes the answer
KL(P ‖ Q) = 0.144
KL(Q ‖ P) = 0.25 × ln ½ + 0.75 × ln 1.5
= −0.173 + 0.304 = 0.131
A real distance is the same both ways.
2 · It can be infinite
G’s coin always lands heads: Q = (1, 0).
tails: 0.5 × ln(0.5 ÷ 0) = ∞
G said “impossible” about something real.
Swapping P and Q swaps the weights: 0.144 vs 0.131.
Divide by 0 → KL = ∞: breaks wish-list rule 4, “finite”.
Why GANs care: early fakes give zero chance to real images, so KL just says ∞, with no direction.

Unit 2 · 24 / 82
04 · Wasserstein loss · sand example 2 / 2
Earth Mover’s distance
Earth Mover’s distance = average move of the cheapest plan
Also called the Wasserstein distance, written W. (Say: “VASS-er-shtine”.)
1
Plan A: 0 → 1, 2 → 5: (1 + 3) ÷ 2 = 2.0. Plan B: 0 → 5, 2 → 1: (5 + 1) ÷ 2 = 3.0.
2
W = the cheaper one = 2.0.
3
Same piles, JS = 0.693: no shared points.
Read W = 2.0 as: “on average, each grain moves 2 steps”.
W = 0 only when the piles are identical.
Why GANs care: W = how far p_g still is from p_data.
Unit 2 · 25 / 82
04 · Wasserstein loss · a shortcut
Slide a whole pile: W = distance
real
fake
every grain: 3 m
Fake pile = real pile, just slid 3 m right.
Cheapest plan: slide it back. Every grain moves 3 m.
So W = 3. Slide by d → W = d.
Why GANs care: W still grows when piles don’t touch.

Unit 2 · 29 / 82
04 · Wasserstein loss · W-loss 1 / 2
The W-loss: just means and minus signs
L_C = − E[C(x)] + E[C(G(z))]
critic: push real scores up, fake scores down
L_G = − E[C(G(z))]
generator: make the critic score fakes high
# critic step
fake  = gen(noise).detach()
loss_C = -critic(real).mean() + critic(fake).mean()
# generator step
fake  = gen(noise)
loss_G = -critic(fake).mean()
No labels, no log, no sigmoid, no BCELoss. Each loss is minimised by its own optimizer: opt_C and opt_G.

04 · Wasserstein loss · W-loss 2 / 2
Both losses on our batch
Critic scores: real 2.0, 1.0, 3.0 · fake −1.0, 0.0, −2.0
1
Means: E[C(x)] = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.0 · E[C(G(z))] = −3 ÷ 3 = −1.0
2
L_C = −2.0 + (−1.0) = −3.0
3
Flip the sign: W estimate = −L_C = 3.0, the real-minus-fake gap.
4
L_G = −(−1.0) = 1.0: G wants to push fake scores up.
Why it matters: −L_C is a W estimate: it falls as G improves, so it tracks quality.

Unit 2 · 33 / 82
05 · Lipschitz & GP · speed limit 1 / 2
The speed limit as a formula
Story so far: The W-loss works only if the critic’s slope stays ≤ 1. Now: how to enforce that limit.
|f(a) − f(b)| ≤ K · |a − b|
“the output gap is at most K times the input gap”
| … | = size of a gap, ignoring the sign.
K = the speed limit (the Lipschitz constant).
K = 1 → we say “1-Lipschitz”.
Check: a = 2, b = 6
Input gap: |2 − 6| = 4
f(x) = 0.5x: outputs 1 and 3, gap 2 ≤ 4 ✓
f(x) = 3x: outputs 6 and 18, gap 12 > 4 ✗
So 0.5x passes; 3x is only 3-Lipschitz.

05 · Lipschitz & GP · the critic’s limit
Many inputs: the gradient’s length
‖∇C(x)‖₂ ≤ 1
“the length of the critic’s gradient is at most 1, everywhere”
∇C = one slope per pixel (the gradient, as in backprop).
‖ ‖₂ = its length, by Pythagoras.
That length = slope in the steepest direction.
Two critics, 2 pixels
C = 0.6x₁ + 0.8x₂ → ∇C = (0.6, 0.8)
Length √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1.0 ✓
C = 3x₁ + 4x₂ → ∇C = (3, 4)
Length √(9 + 16) = 5 ✗ too steep

05 · Lipschitz & GP · three methods
Three ways to enforce the limit
A critic has thousands of weights. How do we keep its slope ≤ 1?
1
Weight clipping
Clamp every weight into a tiny range.
WGAN 2017
2
Gradient penalty
Add a fine when the slope isn’t 1.
WGAN-GP 2017 · we use this
3
Spectral norm
Shrink each layer so it can’t stretch too much.
SN-GAN 2018 · optional

05 · Lipschitz & GP · weight clipping 2 / 2
What weight clipping gets wrong
c too small
c = 0.001: critic too restricted. Gradients vanish through the layers; learning is very slow.
c too large
c = 0.1: gradients explode through the layers; training is unstable.
Capacity lost
Most weights end up exactly at −c or +c: the critic becomes a very simple function.
Still a big step up from BCE. The fix comes next: the gradient penalty.
Why it matters: one number c is hard to pick, so we need a better method.

The penalty formula
GP = average of (‖∇C(x̂)‖₂ − 1)²
“how far each slope is from 1, squared, averaged over the batch”; the fine added is λ · GP
1
Slope length at each x̂
2
Minus 1, then square
3
Average → GP, times λ
λ = 0
No limit: critic scores blow up.
λ = 10
Paper default; we use it.
λ = 1000
Too strong: critic chases the fine, ignores real vs fake.
Unit 2 · 42 / 82
05 · Lipschitz & GP · gradient penalty 3 / 3
The penalty on a batch of four
Given: the section 04 batch, E[C(x̃)] = −1.0 and E[C(x)] = 2.0; λ = 10; the blend x̂ = (−0.1, 0.5).
1
Slope at x̂: ∇C(x̂) = (1.2, 1.6) → √(1.44 + 2.56) = √4 = 2.0
2
The batch’s 4 slopes: 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 1.5 → fines (slope − 1)² = 1, 0, 0.25, 0.25
3
GP = (1 + 0 + 0.25 + 0.25) ÷ 4 = 0.375 → λ · GP = 3.75
4
L_C = −1.0 − 2.0 + 3.75 = 0.75. The slope-2 image alone adds 10 × 1 ÷ 4 = 2.5.
Why it matters: slopes near 1 cost almost nothing; steep slopes are fined.
Unit 2 · 43 / 82
05 · Lipschitz & GP · no BatchNorm
No BatchNorm in the critic
1
BatchNorm averages over the whole batch (Unit 1).
2
So one image’s score depends on the other images.
3
The penalty needs each image’s own slope.
4
Batch mixing spoils that slope.
Use instead

Unit 2 · 45 / 82
06 · WGAN-GP code · 1 / 4
The critic: a scorer, no Sigmoid
class Critic(nn.Module):
    """Scores images. Higher = more realistic. No Sigmoid."""
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            # 1 x 28 x 28
            nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 4, 2, 1),            # -> 64 x 14 x 14
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 4, 2, 1),           # -> 128 x 7 x 7
            nn.InstanceNorm2d(128),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(128 * 7 * 7, 1),             # -> 1 score
            # NO SIGMOID!
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.model(x)

Unit 2 · 47 / 82
06 · WGAN-GP code · the penalty
The gradient_penalty function
Why we need this function: it is the only new code in WGAN-GP.
def gradient_penalty(critic, real, fake, device):
    bs = real.size(0)
    # 1. Random interpolation between real and fake
    epsilon = torch.rand(bs, 1, 1, 1, device=device)   # one per image
    interpolated = (epsilon * real + (1 - epsilon) * fake).requires_grad_(True)
    # 2. Critic scores on interpolated images
    scores = critic(interpolated)
    # 3. Gradients of scores w.r.t. INPUT (not weights!)
    gradients = torch.autograd.grad(
        outputs=scores,
        inputs=interpolated,
        grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(scores),
        create_graph=True,     # need to backprop through this
        retain_graph=True,
    )[0]
    # 4. Penalty: (||gradient||_2 - 1)^2
    gradients = gradients.view(bs, -1)
    penalty = ((gradients.norm(2, dim=1) - 1) ** 2).mean()
    return penalty
1. x̂ = ε · x + (1 − ε) · x̃
2. score each blend
3. slope of the score w.r.t. the pixels
4. length per image, (length − 1)², average
Unit 2 · 48 / 82
06 · WGAN-GP code · 3 / 4
The WGAN-GP loop
for real, _ in loader:          # inside the epoch loop
    real = real.to(device)
    bs = real.size(0)
    for _ in range(n_critic):
        noise = torch.randn(bs, z_dim, device=device)
        fake  = gen(noise).detach()
        gp = gradient_penalty(critic, real, fake, device)
        loss_C = -critic(real).mean() + critic(fake).mean() + lambda_gp * gp
        opt_C.zero_grad()
        loss_C.backward()
        opt_C.step()
        # NO WEIGHT CLIPPING!
    noise = torch.randn(bs, z_dim, device=device)
    fake  = gen(noise)
    loss_G = -critic(fake).mean()
    opt_G.zero_grad()
    loss_G.backward()
    opt_G.step()
New: the gp line and + lambda_gp * gp.
Gone: the clamp loop.
Generator step: unchanged.

Sigmoid left in the critic

Signs swapped

07 · Conditional GAN · feeding D 1 / 2
Why D must see the label too
We ask G for a 7. It draws a perfect 3. What happens?
D without the label
D only asks “does this look like a real digit?”
A perfect 3 → “real!” G is rewarded for ignoring the order.
D with the label
D asks “is this a real 7?”
A perfect 3 → “fake!” G must obey the label to win.
A D that ignores labels → G ignores them too.

07 · Conditional GAN · the cGAN game
The cGAN game: add “| y”
min_G max_D V = E[ log D(x | y) ] + E[ log(1 − D(G(z | y) | y)) ]
D(x | y): “chance x is a real example of class y”.
G(z | y): “the image G draws when asked for y”.
Real pairs (x, y) come from the dataset. For fakes, we choose y.
Same game as Unit 1
D tries to make V big, G tries to make it small. Every D and G just gains “| y”.
Mirza & Osindero, 2014: “Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets”.

08 · Controllable generation · walking 1 / 2
Walking from z1 to z2: lerp
z = (1 − α) · z1 + α · z2,   α from 0 to 1
Recall Unit 1: blend two z’s step by step; each blend → G → one image.
α = 0 → all z1. α = 1 → all z2. α = 0.5 → half and half.
Name: lerp, linear interpolation. “Filling in between” on a straight line.
Check
(1 − α) and α always add to 1.
α = 0.3 → 70% z1 + 30% z2.
Good GAN: every in-between image looks like a real digit. Blurry middles = “holes” in the map.
